On the words 'Our Lord, You made us die twice and gave us life twice', the majority, including Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Kathir, understand two deaths and two lives: existence as dead in the loins of their fathers, life on earth, death, then resurrection. Al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd offer other readings, which Ibn Kathir finds weak since they imply three lives. Al-Razi uses the verse to support the punishment of the grave, a point others dispute. All agree that the question 'Is there any way out?' is a cry of despair, answered by the fact that exit is impossible because they denied God's oneness and associated partners with Him.

This passage records the words of the disbelievers in the Fire, after they have come to loathe themselves. They are told that God's hatred of them, when they were called to faith and refused, is far greater than their own hatred of themselves today. They then say: Our Lord, You made us die twice and gave us life twice; we acknowledge our sins; is there any way out? Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, explain the two deaths as the state of non-existence or of a seed in the loins before birth, followed by ordinary death, and the two lives as life in this world and the resurrection, comparing the verse to al-Baqara 28. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya judge the views of Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi weak because they imply three quickenings. Al-Suddi places the quickenings in the grave for questioning, a point al-Razi uses as evidence for the punishment of the grave and Ibn al-Qayyim discusses at length. Al-Zamakhshari reads one of the deaths as a metaphor. On the plea itself, most hold it is a confession that cannot help them, while Ibn Juzayy and Abu al-Su'ud see in it a hope of gain. Al-Hasan takes the exit to mean a deed that saves, and Qatada a return to the world. The divine reply gives the reason for their fate as their disbelief when God alone is called upon.

This verse describes the fate of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection: after seeing their deeds and the torment of the Fire, they loathe themselves, and they are told that God's loathing of them when they were called to faith and refused was greater than their loathing of themselves today. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that their words 'You made us die twice and gave us life twice' refer to two deaths and two lives, the death before earthly life and the death at its end, followed by resurrection. They then ask to return to the world, and are told there is no way out. Commentators differ on the two deaths: Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take them as being dead in the loins of the fathers and then ordinary death; al-Sudi takes the second life to be in the grave for questioning; Ibn Zayd refers to the covenant taken from Adam's back. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya consider the last two views weak, since they imply three lives. The phrase 'the Most High, the Most Great' is explained by God's absolute authority and the greatness of His judgment, and al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya stress that these are praises that do not concern place. Al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi report that the Kharijites relied on 'judgment belongs to God alone', and that 'Ali replied it was a true word used to convey falsehood. The following verses speak of God's signs and call for sincere worship.

The commentators explain that God shows His servants His signs, meaning the proofs of His oneness and power. These include the winds, clouds, thunder and lightning, the miracles of the prophets and the verses of the Quran. He also sends down provision from the sky. Most take this provision to be rain, since it is the cause of sustenance, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi state. Ibn 'Atiyya widens the word to include decrees and judgment. The remembrance meant is reflection and admonition, which reaches only the one who turns back to God in repentance and obedience, as as-Sudi and az-Zamakhshari note. The scholars then agree that the believers are commanded to call upon God alone with sincere devotion, even if the disbelievers dislike it, that is to worship God without associating others with Him. The main disagreement concerns the link between the two gifts. Al-Razi holds that the signs nourish the hearts and the provision nourishes the bodies, while others mention only the rain as a gift. Ibn Sa'di draws the conclusion that every blessing, spiritual or material, comes from God. No legal ruling is drawn from these commentaries.

This verse commands believers to worship God alone, devoting their religion sincerely to Him and free of any association, even if the disbelievers are displeased. Most commentators understand the word 'invoke' as meaning worship, though some include supplication as well. The majority link the command to the verses before it, in which God shows His signs and sends down provision from the sky, and only the one who turns back to Him truly takes heed. Al-Tabari and al-Suddi explain 'the one who turns in repentance' as the one who returns to obedience and to the oneness of God, a view also held by Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi add that sincerity means purifying the act for God, and that the disbelievers deeply hate it. Ibn Kathir also cites the hadith from Ibn al-Zubayr about the words of remembrance after the prescribed prayers. Ibn 'Ashur sees the command as following from what the believers have witnessed, and understands the disbelievers' displeasure as opposition and an attempt to turn believers away, so the meaning is steadfastness in worship at all times. Modern commentators such as al-Sha'rawi connect sincere supplication with humility before God, which irritates those who were arrogant toward Him. Ibn 'Uthaymin defines sincerity as purifying worship from association, counts ostentation as a lesser form of shirk, and holds that it invalidates the act if it takes hold. The commentators agree on the core message: remain steadfast in monotheism without caring about the anger of those who associate partners with God.

The commentators explain that this verse describes God as exalted in degrees, lord of the Throne, who sends down the Spirit, meaning the revelation that gives life to hearts, by His command upon whomever He wills among His servants, so that He may warn of the Day of Meeting, which is the Day of Resurrection. Most agree that the "meeting" refers to the encounter of the inhabitants of heaven and earth, or of the creature with the Creator, or of the oppressor with the oppressed. The verse prepares the description of the Day of Exposure, when people appear with nothing concealing them and nothing is hidden from God. On "exalted in degrees", Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr take it to mean the heavens raised one above another, others take it as the greatness of God's attributes or the elevated ranks of the righteous in Paradise. Qatada and al-Suddi understand the "Spirit" as revelation or prophethood, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd as the Quran, al-Dahhak as Gabriel, and al-Hasan as mercy; al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi stress that it gives life to hearts as the spirit gives life to bodies. As for "by His command", some read it as His word, His decree, or His cause. The readings of "that he may warn" may refer back to God or to the Messenger. On the Day of Exposure, the commentators say people will come out of their graves in plain view; God asks, to whom belongs the dominion today, and answers Himself: to God, the One, the Subduer, though some hold that the assembly answers. The exegetes add that each soul is repaid for what it earned, that no one is wronged that day, and that the reckoning is swift.

This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when all creatures will stand exposed before God, with nothing to conceal them, and nothing about them or their deeds hidden from Him. Then comes the call, "To whom belongs the dominion today?", and God answers Himself: "To God, the One, the Subduer." The commentators agree that the whole scene belongs to the Last Day, and they understand "exposed" as standing on a bare plain with no mountain, tree or building to shelter anyone, as al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report from Ibn Mas'ud and others. Opinions differ on who calls and who answers. Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes, as al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir relate, hold that God speaks when no one remains after the creatures have perished, and answers Himself. Al-Hasan says the one who asks is also the one who answers, while Ibn Jurayj holds that all creatures answer together. Ibn Mas'ud reports that a herald calls out and the people of the gathering reply. Al-Zamakhshari and others take the verse as a report of what is said on that day. Some, such as al-Mawardi, read "nothing is hidden from Him" as a warning of requital, while al-Tabari stresses that God knows all at all times, but that on that day people who thought they were hidden in this world discover they were not. From the verse the exegetes draw the principle that each soul will be repaid for what it has earned, which some connect with their doctrine of acquisition of acts, though the commentators do not all agree on the details.

This verse states that on the Day of Judgment every soul will be repaid for what it earned, good or bad, with no injustice, and that God is swift in reckoning. According to al-Tabari, every doer will receive the reward of his deeds: no one's good will be diminished, and no one will bear another's sin. He also reports that this day will not reach its midpoint before the people of Paradise have rested in Paradise and the people of the Fire in the Fire. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur agree that the repayment will be perfectly just, and that the swiftness of the reckoning comes from God being occupied by no affair that distracts Him from another and needing neither counting nor reflection, so that He judges all creatures at once. Ibn Kathir and al-Samani specify that the injustice ruled out covers adding bad deeds or subtracting good ones. Ibn 'Ashur sees the phrase 'God is swift in reckoning' as the reason both for the repayment and for the absence of injustice. Opinions differ on how long the reckoning takes: al-Dahhak places it between two prayers, others at the length of a sip of water, while al-Samani, citing al-Dahhak and others, speaks of roughly half a day of our time. Ibn 'Atiyya reads the verse as establishing that reward and punishment depend on what the servant has acquired. Al-Razi draws from it that complete recompense takes place only on the Day of Resurrection, and builds on the verse legal principles concerning harms and penalties. Al-Qurtubi and al-Samani also report that the first matters judged among people will be cases of bloodshed.

God tells His Prophet to warn people of the Day of Resurrection, called al-Azifa because it is near, since everything that is coming is near. The commentators describe the state of creation on that day: hearts rise from the chests into the throats out of terror, neither returning to their places nor leaving, while people are overwhelmed with distress and fall silent. They all agree that the wrongdoers, meaning the polytheists, will have no close friend who cares for them and no intercessor whose intercession is accepted. The meaning of "yuta" (obeyed) is disputed, however. Al-Tabari and al-Samarqandi take it to mean the intercessor is not granted what he asks, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that the negation covers both the intercession and its acceptance, and Ibn 'Atiyya reads it as negating intercession itself. Al-Qurtubi notes the wording may also suggest intercessors who are not heeded. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari report that the Mu'tazilites used the verse to deny intercession for grave sinners, and the Sunni scholars reply that the denial concerns only unbelievers. The following verses state that God knows the stealthy glance of the eyes and what the breasts conceal, that He judges with truth, and that the idols decide nothing. The commentators finally recall the fate of earlier peoples destroyed for their sins.

This verse states that God knows what human eyes steal in furtive glances and what hearts conceal. The commentators agree that the 'treachery of the eyes' means a stolen look at what is forbidden: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada describe it as a glance taken unnoticed by those present, while al-Dahhak understands it as saying 'I saw' when one has not seen. As for what the breasts conceal, as-Suddi explains it as whisperings of the soul, Ibn Abbas as the intention to commit adultery if one were able, and al-Mawardi as whatever the heart keeps of trust or betrayal. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di see in it the basis of divine justice: God judges with truth, rewarding good with good and evil with evil, whereas the idols invoked besides Him decide nothing, having neither knowledge nor power. Readers differ on the verb 'call upon': the Medinan reading uses the second person, the majority of Kufan readers the third, and al-Tabari holds both to be correct. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya discuss how the verse connects to its context, some linking it to swift reckoning and others to divine knowledge. Al-Razi counts it among the causes of dread on the Day of Judgment, since a judge who knows every hidden thing inspires in the guilty a fear beyond measure.

This part of the verse states that God alone judges with truth and justice, while the idols and false gods worshipped besides Him do not judge anything, since they know nothing and have no power; therefore they do not deserve worship. The verse closes by affirming that God is the All-Hearing and the All-Seeing, Who will recompense people for their deeds. The commentators agree that the judgment mentioned concerns the recompense, whether good or bad. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi explain that denying the idols any power to judge is a form of mockery and shows their helplessness; one cannot even say of them that they judge or do not judge. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur stress that the sentence emphasises that true judgment belongs to God alone, and that He does not err. The main difference concerns the reading of the verb 'yad'ūna', with ya or ta. Al-Tabari notes that most readers of Kufa read it with ya, while the readers of Medina read it with ta, and he considers both readings correct and equivalent in meaning. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take the subject of the verb to be the disbelievers, whereas Ibn Kathir extends it to anything worshipped besides God. Al-Zamakhshari sees in the closing phrase both a warning to the disbelievers and an allusion to the idols' inability to hear or see. Overall, the commentators agree that justice belongs to God alone and that whatever is worshipped beside Him is powerless.

In this verse God urges the Meccan disbelievers to travel through the earth and reflect on the fate of the peoples who came before them. Those peoples were stronger and left more lasting traces on the land, in buildings, fortresses and settlements, yet God seized them for their sins, meaning their disbelief, their denial and the wrongs they had committed, and they had no one to shield them from God's punishment. Commentators such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya agree that this journey is one of reflection and learning, and that the fate of these peoples is a warning to the Quraysh. Al-Tabari explains that strength refers to physical power and bodily size, and that the traces are the buildings and dwellings. Al-Mawardi lists five possible meanings of the traces, including edifices, the ruin and cultivation of the land, walking on foot and long life. Al-Zamakhshari suggests the phrase may mean 'more traces' and cites a line of poetry in support. Ibn 'Amir's reading, 'minkum' with the kaf, differs from the majority reading 'minhum'. Al-Razi clarifies that the waqi is the protector who shields, and connects the verse to the threat of worldly punishment following the warning of the Hereafter. The next verse explains that the cause of the punishment was the sending of messengers with clear proofs, which these peoples rejected. These commentaries mention no legal rulings in connection with this verse and focus on the lesson and the warning.

The commentators explain that this verse (40:22) gives the reason for the destruction of earlier peoples: their messengers had brought them clear proofs, yet they rejected them, and God seized them in punishment. He is mighty and His punishment is severe. Most read the word 'that' as referring to the retribution that struck the disbelieving nations, and see the verse as preparing a warning to the Quraysh to take heed of what befell their predecessors. On the general meaning there is broad agreement: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God destroyed those nations after giving them warning, that their strength and monuments did not protect them, and that no one can repel His decree. Al-Tabari sees a threat addressed to the polytheists of Quraysh, while Ibn 'Atiyya reads it both as consolation for the Prophet and as a lesson for the Quraysh, leading into the story of Moses. The commentators differ on the phrase 'traces in the land': Mujahid takes them to be ruins and buildings, Ibn Jurayj walking on foot, al-Kalbi the pursuit taken to its end, Muqatil long lives, and al-Mawardi the good and bad customs they established. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report these variant readings. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the strength meant is largely moral, namely numbers and resources. Ibn 'Uthaymin stresses that visiting the ruins should be an act of reflection rather than mere sightseeing.

God tells us that He sent Moses with His signs and a clear authority to Pharaoh, Haman and Qarun, and they called him a lying sorcerer. The verse consoles the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ by showing that earlier messengers faced the same rejection. The commentators agree that the signs are the miracles, such as the staff and the hand, and that the manifest authority is the clear proof. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the opponents labelled the miracle as sorcery and Moses as an impostor who lied about God. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that Pharaoh, Haman and Qarun are named because they led the hostility against Moses, and most hold that Qarun was from the Children of Israel, though Ibn 'Atiyya questions whether he was the well-known Qarun. Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas report that Pharaoh had stopped killing boys but then ordered their killing again after Moses came. The readings differ on the particles and vowels of the words for the decree and corruption, without changing the core meaning. The exegetes conclude that the verse promises victory to the believers and warns the disbelievers that their scheming will be lost.

God says that He sent Moses with His clear signs and manifest authority to Pharaoh, Haman and Qarun. When they could not withstand the proof, they called him a magician and a liar. The commentators explain that Haman was Pharaoh's minister and Qarun the man of great wealth, and that they are named together because they were the most prominent figures in opposing Moses. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Qatada see the verse as consolation for the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, facing the rejection of his own people, with the assurance that the final victory belongs to the believers. The word 'magician' means, in their view, that they attributed the miracles to sorcery, and 'liar' that they denied his divine mission. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that the killing of the boys and the sparing of the girls mentioned afterwards was a renewed persecution after Moses' mission, distinct from the earlier one before his birth, as Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada state. Al-Razi adds that the sons were targeted because they might strengthen Moses, while the daughters posed no such threat. On Haman, al-Sam'ani cites al-Dahhak's view that he was neither Israelite nor Coptic, and defends the possibility that another man bore that name. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that Qarun might be a different person from the Qarun of the Children of Israel, but most identify them as the same. Readers also differ on whether the particle in the following verse is read as 'or' or 'and', which changes the grammar but leaves the meaning largely the same.

This verse describes how Pharaoh and his chiefs responded when Moses brought them the truth and the clear signs from Allah. Unable to answer with argument, they ordered that the sons of those who believed with Moses be killed and their women spared for service and humiliation. The commentators agree that this killing was different from the first one, which had been carried out before Moses was born. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report, citing Qatada and Ibn Abbas, that Pharaoh had stopped killing the infant boys and that, when Moses was sent, he renewed the killing out of rage and fear. Regarding the word kayd, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand it as the scheming and plotting of the disbelievers, whose end is perdition and failure, fi dalal, meaning loss and vanishing. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan add that their scheme turned back against them and did not succeed. Ibn Ashur notes that the plan was first held in secret and then set aside because of the disasters that struck them. All the commentators see in this verse a consolation for the Prophet and a warning to the Quraysh: the schemes of the disbelievers always fail.

This verse reports Pharaoh's words to his court: leave me to kill Moses, and let him call upon his Lord; I fear that he will change your religion or that he will spread corruption in the land. The commentators agree that Pharaoh wanted to give the impression that his people were holding him back, while in truth he feared Moses' mission. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, citing Qatada, note that this order to kill is distinct from the earlier slaughter of the newborn boys and was a renewed command. The meaning of 'your religion' is debated: al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take it to mean the worship of Pharaoh and of idols, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya understands it as authority and rule, citing a line of Zuhayr. Al-Zamakhshari holds that the 'corruption' means strife and disorder that destroy security and livelihoods, while al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir link it both to the loss of religion and to the disruption of life. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi read 'let him call upon his Lord' as mockery and a challenge. Ibn 'Ashur explains that 'leave me' expresses a declared intention. The recitations differ between 'wa-anna' and 'aw anna', and between 'yuzhira' and 'yazhara', but the commentators judge that these variants do not change the general meaning. The core of the passage remains Pharaoh's threat against Moses, justified by fear of losing power and the established order.

The commentators explain that when Moses heard Pharaoh threaten to kill him, he sought refuge with God, saying that he takes refuge in his Lord and the Lord of his people from every arrogant person who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya agree that arrogance means refusing to submit to the truth and looking down on people, and that disbelief in the Day of Reckoning, added to it, brings a person to the height of cruelty and audacity against God and His servants. Moses does not name Pharaoh but uses a general description that includes him and every other tyrant, as al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur point out; Ibn 'Ashur adds that the words were addressed to his own people to reassure them. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that attaching the Lord to both himself and his people encourages them to follow his example in seeking refuge in God. The readings of 'udhtu, with or without assimilation of the letters, are mentioned by Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud without any effect on the meaning. Regarding the preceding verses, al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi take the corruption Pharaoh feared to mean the change of his people's religion and the worship of other than God, whereas al-Razi sees in it both the corruption of religion and the corruption of worldly affairs. All agree that seeking refuge means turning to God and placing one's trust in Him in times of hardship.

The Qur'an here reports the words of a believing man from Pharaoh's household who was concealing his faith. He rebukes Pharaoh and his chiefs for wanting to kill a man whose only offence is to say "My Lord is God", when he has brought clear proofs from their Lord. The commentators generally take the plain sense to be that this man was a relative of Pharaoh or part of his court, and that he kept his faith secret out of fear for himself; he had not harmed Moses because he had listened to him and held back from killing him. They differ on his name, with Habib, Hizqil and Hizbil among the names given, none firmly established, and a minority, including al-Tabari, rejecting the view that he was an Israelite. He then argues by alternatives: if Moses is lying, the lie falls on him alone; if he is truthful, some of what he promises will strike them. Several scholars explain that saying "some" is a gentle way of addressing the audience and conceding ground in argument, though some take "some" to mean all. The closing words about the prodigal liar are read by some as referring to Moses, spoken in argument, and by others as referring to Pharaoh, who exceeds bounds in killing and lies in claiming lordship. Commentators also differ on the meaning of excess: Qatada took it as polytheism, al-Suddi as unjust killing, and al-Tabari concluded that both are included. Some compare this man's stance with that of Abu Bakr when he defended the Prophet, while noting that one hid his faith and the other proclaimed it.

This verse records the words of the believing man from Pharaoh's household, who addresses his people: the kingdom is yours today, and you hold dominance in the land of Egypt, but who would defend us against the punishment of God if it came upon us? Pharaoh replies that he shows them only what he himself sees and guides them only to the path of right guidance. The commentators differ on who this man was. Al-Suddi, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that he was a cousin of Pharaoh of Coptic origin who was saved along with Moses, a view that Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi largely share. Al-Hasan holds that he believed before Moses arrived, while Ibn Abbas and others give different names, such as Habib or Hizqil. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya read Pharaoh's words as concealment and deception, since he sensed the fear that Moses inspired. Ibn Kathir notes the hadith of Abu Bakr defending the Prophet with this verse, and Ibn Ashur stresses the gentle address "O my people" as a rhetorical method. On recitation, most read "al-rashad" with a single consonant, while Mu'adh ibn Jabal read it with a doubled consonant, a reading others consider a mistake.

The verse reports the words of the believing man from Pharaoh's family, who warns his people against killing Moses and makes them fear a fate like that of the peoples who banded together against their prophets: the punishment that struck Noah's people, 'Ad, Thamud and those after them. The commentators agree that the 'Day of the Confederates' means the days on which those peoples were destroyed; the singular 'day' and the plural 'confederates' are explained as a compact expression, and 'like the custom of Noah's people' clarifies that it means the retribution for their persistence in disbelief and denial. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that 'God does not desire injustice for His servants' means God destroys no one except for their sins and after the proof has been established, so the destruction was just. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that denying the will to do injustice is stronger than denying injustice itself, and al-Zamakhshari adds that Ahl al-Sunna distinguish will from approval. Al-Razi reads the passage as a model of a man who protects a preacher without being related to him. As for 'the Day of Calling', most take it to be the Day of Resurrection when people call out to one another, while Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and others read it as 'tanadd', meaning flight, which al-Nahhas also favours. Commentators differ on the man's name and his kinship to Pharaoh's family: Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil name him Hizqil, and the majority identify him with the believer already mentioned.

The commentators explain that the believer from Pharaoh's household, having advised his people not to kill Moses, warned them about the fate of earlier nations who denied their prophets. He feared for them "a day like that of the factions," meaning the days of destruction of the groups that banded together against God's messengers: the people of Noah, ʿAd, Thamud, and those after them. The phrase "like the custom of" refers to the punishment earned by their persistence in disbelief and denial until the chastisement fell upon them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that God did not destroy them unjustly but because of their sins, after proof had been established against them, and that the words "God does not desire injustice for His servants" mean that He punishes no one without fault or before the proof is conveyed. Al-Zamakhshari holds that this negation is stronger than a plain denial of injustice, while Ibn ʿAtiyya reads it as a denial that God Himself would wrong them. Al-Zamakhshari reports that the Mu'tazila take the word "desire" to mean approval, whereas the People of the Sunna affirm that God wills what He creates without approving of evil. Some readers pronounce "al-tanad" as the day of calling out, others as the day of flight and dispersal, and some with a doubled consonant. Ibn ʿAshur holds that injustice includes association with God and wronging others, and that the negation covers both. Ibn ʿUthaymin draws from the passage that God does not will injustice because of the perfection of His justice.

The commentators explain that the believing man from Pharaoh's household warns his people about the Day of Tanad, that is the Day of Resurrection. They differ on the meaning of the name. Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj hold that people call out to one another on that day, the people of Paradise calling to the people of the Fire and the reverse, as described in Surat al-A'raf. Ibn Jurayj also reports that the damned cry out woe and destruction. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir note that the name may gather all these meanings, and they cite a hadith from Abu Hurayra about the trumpet of terror, in which people flee calling to one another. Those who read the word with a doubled dal, such as Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak, take it to mean flight and scattering, like camels that bolt, and they link to this sense the words 'the day you turn your backs in flight'. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir mention other readings, but all agree the verse speaks of the Day of Judgment. The commentators also stress that no one can protect a person from God, and that whom God leads astray has no guide. The readings differ on whether the final yā is written, most omitting it while Ibn Kathir keeps it.

This verse reports the words of the believing man from Pharaoh's household to his people: on the day you turn your backs in flight, no one will protect you from God, and whomever God leads astray has no guide. The commentators agree that the Day of Calling (yawm al-tanād) is the Day of Resurrection, but they differ on the meaning of the word. The majority reading, al-tanād with a light dal, is explained by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir as the mutual calling between the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, as described in Surat al-Aʿraf. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi add that people will cry out to one another in lamentation, and Ibn Kathir considers combining all these calls a good view. Al-Qurtubi also notes that proclamations of felicity or wretchedness will be made at the weighing of deeds. A variant attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak reads al-tannādd with a doubled dal, meaning flight, as a camel bolts from its herders. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir report this sense, and al-Alusi prefers it because it links with the phrase about having no protector. On the phrase « turning your backs » (mudbirīn), Qatada takes it to mean departing from the place of judgment toward the Fire, while Mujahid and as-Suddi understand a flight away from the Fire. Al-Tabari gives weight to the prophetic report from Abu Hurayra on the blast of terror and considers Qatada's view not far from the truth. The word ʿāṣim means one who protects or prevents, and the commentators agree that no one can shield the people from God's punishment.

The verse records the words of the believing man from Pharaoh's household, who reminds his people that Joseph son of Jacob had come to them before Moses with clear proofs, and that they remained in doubt about what he brought. When Joseph died, they said that God would never send another messenger after him; so, the verse concludes, God leads astray whoever is wanton and doubting. Most commentators understand the address as directed at the ancestors, to whom the present audience is linked, and identify Joseph as the son of Jacob, who according to al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Sam'ani remained among his people for twenty years after his father's death. Al-Mawardi and al-Naqqash report, through al-Dahhak, an opinion that the messenger was a jinn named Joseph, but al-Sam'ani calls this weak since the unqualified name refers to the well-known Joseph. Ibn Jurayj takes the proofs to be the dream interpretation, while Ibn al-Sa'ib mentions interpreting dreams and the tearing of the shirt. The phrase 'God will never send a messenger' is read by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi as a rejection of Joseph's mission and of any successor, whereas Ibn 'Ashur argues that the verse implies Joseph was indeed a messenger. Regarding the Pharaoh, Wahb ibn Munabbih holds that he was Moses' Pharaoh, who lived a very long life, while others consider him a different ruler, and al-Sha'rawi places Joseph in the era of the Hyksos. Minor variant readings do not change the core meaning. The commentators agree that the misguidance is a punishment for excess and doubt, and that the arrogant tyrant has his heart sealed.

This verse describes those who dispute the signs of God without any authority, and the commentators agree that their disputing is greatly hateful to God and to the believers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy explain that the hatred (maqt) is intense aversion, along with the punishment that follows, and that the disputing meant is that of denial and falsehood rather than argument backed by proof. Most take these words to be spoken by the believer from Pharaoh's family, who warns his people of the fate of earlier nations and of the Day of Calling, after recalling the coming of Joseph. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi link the closing phrases to the unbelief of Joseph's people after his death, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi treat them as a lasting description. On the reading, al-Tabari, Abu Ubayd and al-Zajjaj prefer the construct form "every heart of a proud one", whereas Abu Amr and Ibn Amir read "qalbin" with tanwin and make the adjectives describe the heart, since the heart is the seat of pride, as al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain. Al-Razi adds that "jabbar" means one who compels others, and Ibn Kathir cites the view that a jabbar is one who kills two people, though this is not offered as a general rule. Ibn Ashur understands the sealing as the creation of misguidance within the heart.

God relates that Pharaoh told his minister Haman to build him a lofty tower so that he might reach the ways of the heavens, look upon the god of Moses, and that he thought Moses was a liar. The commentators agree that Pharaoh meant this to deceive his people and turn them from the truth, and that his scheme could only lead to loss and error. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the asbab are the paths or gates leading to the heavens, while Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take them to be gates, and al-Mawardi takes them as any means of reaching a goal. On the word sarh, al-Hasan understands an assembly hall, al-Suddi a palace, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr baked brick; Ibn Kathir reports from al-Nakha'i that people disliked building with brick and placing it in their graves. Regarding the claim that he thinks Moses a liar, al-Mawardi offers two readings: either ignorance overcame Pharaoh, or he said it to mislead his people while knowing it was impossible. Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the majority read fa-attali'u in the nominative, while Hafs and others read it in the subjunctive, a usage the Basran grammarians rejected and the Kufans accepted. For wa suddda, the readings differ: in the passive, Pharaoh was turned from the path; in the active, he turned others from it. Nearly all commentators take tabab to mean loss and ruin.

This verse records Pharaoh's command to his minister Haman to build him a tall tower so that he might reach the means of access to the heavens, look upon the god of Moses, and his claim that he thinks Moses is a liar. It adds that the evil of his deeds was made attractive to him and he was turned from the path, and that Pharaoh's scheming led only to ruin. The commentators agree on the plain sense: the sarh is a lofty, conspicuous building. As for the 'asbab al-samawat', al-Sudi and Abu Salih take them to be the ways of the heavens, Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas the gates of the heavens, while others read them as the stages between the heavens; al-Zamakhshari notes that whatever leads one to a thing is a means to it, which brings these senses together.

Ibn Kathir and others report that the tower was built of fired brick, and Ibn al-Jawzi names Haman as the first to fire clay, while al-Mawardi lists four meanings of sarh, one of them brick. On 'I think he is a liar', al-Tabari and al-Nasafi explain it as Pharaoh's rejection of Moses' claim that his Lord is in the heavens and sent him. Al-Mawardi offers two readings: either ignorance overcame Pharaoh, or he said it as a deception towards his people while knowing it was impossible, a view attributed to al-Hasan al-Basri.

The nominative reading of 'fa-attali'' is the common one, while the subjunctive reading, attributed to Hafs and al-A'raj, is discussed. For 'wa suddda 'an al-sabil', the readers differ between active and passive voice, and commentators understand it either as God's action through causation or as Pharaoh turning people from the path. Finally, 'tabab' is unanimously taken to mean loss and ruin, as confirmed by al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir.

The believer from Pharaoh's family addresses his people, urging them to follow him, because he will guide them to the path of right guidance, meaning the religion brought by Moses and the way to salvation. He then turns them away from the present life, describing it as a brief and passing enjoyment, and encourages them toward the hereafter, which he presents as the lasting abode. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the hereafter is the abode of settling because its people, in paradise or in hell, never leave it. Al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report that the following verses develop this summary: whoever does an evil deed is repaid only with its equal, while whoever does righteous deeds while believing enters paradise and is provided for without reckoning. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that this speech follows Pharaoh's claim that he shows them only the right path, and they read it as an indirect rebuttal of that claim. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that rashad is the opposite of misguidance, and that the phrase contains a near-explicit hint that the path of Pharaoh and his people is the path of error. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, attribute these words to the believing man of Pharaoh's family, while some, such as al-Nasafi, mention other views on the speaker. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the speech moves from a general statement to its details in order to hold the listeners' attention. Al-Qurtubi notes that Mu'adh ibn Jabal read rashad with a shadda, a reading that most grammarians consider incorrect.

In this verse, the believer from Pharaoh's household tells his people that the life of this world is only a brief and passing enjoyment, while the Hereafter is the abode of lasting stability. The commentators read the message as a call to turn away from what passes and to work for what endures. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Baghawi agree that "the Hereafter" means Paradise and Hellfire, since neither of them perishes, and that "mata'" is a limited enjoyment that comes to an end. Al-Tabari also reports, through Qatada, that Paradise settles with its people and the Fire with its own.

Most commentators treat the verse as an introduction to what follows, where the believer details the fate of the evil deed and of the good deed. Al-Zamakhshari sees in it a correction of the hearts of those who take this world for a permanent home. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the believer built on a belief his people already held, that a life after this one exists. Ibn 'Uthaymin stresses that detachment from this world goes together with longing for the Hereafter.

Ibn al-Qayyim adds that enjoying the pleasures of this world is not blameworthy when they help one reach those of the Hereafter. Al-Qurtubi emphasizes that the abode of the Hereafter is the place where one does not leave, whether it is Paradise or the Fire.

The commentators explain that this verse sets out the principle of recompense: whoever does an evil deed will be repaid only with its equal, while whoever does a righteous deed, male or female, and is a believer, will enter Paradise and be given provision there without reckoning. Al-Tabari and those who follow him take the evil deed to mean associating partners with God or, more broadly, disobedience, and the righteous deed to mean obedience and abstaining from what God forbids; they add that this provision is not measured by any measure or scale. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi stress that the punishment for evil is proportioned to it, whereas the believer's reward is endless and unlimited. Qatada defines the evil deed as shirk, and several scholars follow him. Ibn al-Jawzi reports two views: that it is shirk, or sins in general, and that the righteous deed is either monotheism or obedience in general. Al-Zamakhshari distinguishes the two cases: exceeding the due punishment for evil would be wrong, while exceeding the reward for good is a favour. Ibn 'Ashur sees the mention of faith as a condition for the deed to count, and reads disbelief as a lasting evil that calls for everlasting punishment. Al-Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin conclude that deeds are accepted only when done sincerely and in accordance with the revealed law, and that men and women are equal in recompense. The disagreement thus centres mainly on how to define evil and righteous deeds, and no single view is preferred here.

The Qur'an reports the words of the believing man from Pharaoh's household, who wonders at the situation of his people: how can he call them to salvation by believing in God and following Moses, while they call him to the Fire through disbelief and association. Most commentators understand salvation as faith and good deeds, and the Fire as the association that deserves it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God is the Mighty in His vengeance on His enemies and the Forgiver of those who repent, and al-Tabari adds that idols neither benefit nor harm and do not answer their worshippers. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the phrase "la jarama" as meaning "truly" or "there is no doubt," and they take the denial of knowledge to mean that the idols have no share in divinity at all. Regarding who the "transgressors" are, most identify them as polytheists, while Mujahid and al-Sha'bi identify them as those who shed blood unjustly. As for the speaker, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya take him to be the believer from Pharaoh's household, while others, such as al-Razi, who discusses the matter at length, mention Moses. On the phrase "you will remember what I say to you," some take it to refer to the Hereafter and others to the moment the punishment comes. The commentators largely agree on a call to faith, a warning against polytheism, and the conduct of a believer who advises his people while trusting in God.

The Quran here reports the words of the believer from Pharaoh's household to his people: he asks how he can call them to salvation, meaning belief in God and following Moses, while they call him to the Fire, that is, to disbelief and to the deeds of its people. He details what they urge him to do, namely to disbelieve in God and to associate with Him what he has no knowledge of, and sets against this his own call to the Mighty, the Forgiver. The commentators agree that salvation means escape from God's punishment and that the call to the Fire is a call to its people's deeds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi state that the idols answer no one in this world or the next, and Ibn Kathir adds that the worship is without proof. As for the transgressors, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi take them to be polytheists, while Mujahid and al-Sha'bi understand them as those who shed blood unjustly, and 'Ikrima as arrogant tyrants; al-Qurtubi suggests these meanings all fall under excess. On the phrase la jarama, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi differ, most of them taking it to mean certainly or truly. On the fate of Pharaoh's household, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy report that the believer was saved with Moses, and that their souls are exposed to the Fire morning and evening until the Hour; Ibn Kathir draws from this the punishment of the grave, while Ibn 'Ashur reads the passage more figuratively. Regarding the reading of the verb of entering, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi note both the imperative addressed to the angels and that addressed to Pharaoh's people, without deciding between them.

The commentators explain that the believer from Pharaoh's household tells his people that the idols they call him to worship deserve no worship, since they answer no one who calls on them in this world or the next, that all people return to God, and that those who exceed the limits in disbelief and sin are the companions of the Fire. Most agree that "la jarama" means "certainly" or "without doubt", and that the "call" here is the call to worship: the idols do not summon people to themselves nor respond to those who invoke them. Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Abbas, joined by al-Kalbi, explain that they neither benefit nor harm nor intercede, while al-Suddi says they do not answer their worshippers. Al-Tabari concludes that the "transgressors" are the polytheists, and Ibn Kathir reads the verse the same way, whereas Mujahid and Ibn Mas'ud take them to be those who shed blood unjustly, and Ikrima to be the arrogant tyrants.

The verse also raises the question of the souls of Pharaoh's people being exposed to the Fire morning and evening. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Suddi report that their souls are in the bellies of black birds, and Ibn Kathir treats the verse as evidence, in the view of the Sunnis, for punishment in the grave. Others note that this exposure may concern the soul alone. Al-Tabari reports that the believer was saved with Moses when he crossed the sea, while Muqatil says he fled to a mountain where his pursuers could not reach him. On the phrase "you will remember", Ibn Atiyya and al-Tabari see a threat that may be fulfilled in this world when punishment arrives or in the next, and Ibn Zayd applies it to the next world.

The believing man from Pharaoh's household tells his people that they will remember his advice when they witness the punishment, though that remembrance will then be of no benefit, and that he entrusts his affair to God, who is seeing of His servants. The commentators agree that these are the words of this believer, who had been calling his people to salvation. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the remembrance to occur both in this world and in the Hereafter, while al-Naqqash limits it to the moment the punishment descends, and Ibn Zayd reports that it refers to the Day of Resurrection. Most explain tafwid, entrusting one's affair to God, as surrender and reliance on Him. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan connect the phrase to the threat made against him, while al-Baghawi and Ibn Atiyya report that he spoke after they threatened to kill him. Most attribute the speech to the believer, though a minority hold it was Moses who spoke. The passage goes on to say that God protected him from his people's schemes and that the household of Pharaoh suffered a terrible punishment. Commentators relate that they are displayed to the Fire morning and evening, a report that the people of the Sunna cite as evidence for the punishment of the grave. They differ on how this happens: according to Ibn Mas'ud their souls are in black birds, while some hold that the soul alone is affected and not the body.

The commentators explain that God protected the believer from the family of Pharaoh from the worst of the schemes devised against him and the torments they intended for him, and saved him along with Moses when they crossed the sea, while the evil punishment fell upon Pharaoh and his people. They differ over who was saved. Qatada and Ibn Zayd, among others, take the believer himself to be meant, whereas as-Suddi and some others hold that the pronoun refers to Moses. The majority favour the believer, and some report that he fled to a mountain where he prayed, and that God shielded him when Pharaoh sent men to seize him. As for the phrase 'the family of Pharaoh', most understand it as his people and followers, while at-Tabari and others extend it to Pharaoh himself. The 'evil punishment' is taken by some to be drowning, and by others to be drowning, killing and fire together. The commentators agree that 'they are exposed to the Fire morning and evening' refers to the presentation of their souls to the Fire in the intermediate state, and many cite it as evidence for the punishment of the grave, whereas al-Farra' suggests an inversion and a reference to the Hereafter. They also differ over the reading of 'adkhilu': with a hamza it is a command to the angels to admit them, without it it is addressed to the family of Pharaoh. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim discuss at length whether the punishment falls on the soul alone or on the body with it, drawing on authentic hadiths. Most agree that the final clause points to the greater torment of the Day of Resurrection.

The verse says that the people of Pharaoh are exposed to the Fire morning and evening, and that on the Day the Hour arrives it will be said: admit the people of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and others report that this exposure takes place in the interval after death, and that their souls are placed in the bellies of black birds that go to the Fire and return, as related from Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil. Several commentators, including al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir, state that this verse is a basis for the belief in punishment in the grave, which the People of the Sunna cite. Others, such as Qatada, understand the exposure as a rebuke, with the people being told that these are their dwellings. Al-Tabari notes that morning and evening may refer to the duration of the worldly life. Ibn 'Ashur sees the passage as describing a punishment before the Last Day. Opinions differ on the meaning of the morning and evening: some take them as two fixed moments, others as an expression of continuity, and al-Farra' proposes a reordering of the verse which others reject. Readers differ on the form of the verb adkhilu: some read it as an imperative addressed to the angels, others as an imperative addressed to the people of Pharaoh. On the phrase hāqa bi-āli Fir'awn sū'u al-'adhāb, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur take it as drowning in this world, while al-Zamakhshari takes it more broadly. Commentators agree on the exemplary character of the verse, which shows the fate of the arrogant who reject the messengers.

This verse describes a dispute among the people of the Fire: the weak, meaning the followers, tell their proud leaders that they used to follow them and ask whether they can bear for them a portion of the punishment. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that the followers had obeyed their leaders in disbelief and error, and that the leaders reply that all of them are in the Fire and that God has judged among the servants, giving each his due. The commentators agree that this exchange brings no relief and that no one can lighten another's punishment. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir then report that the damned ask the guardians of Hell to plead with God for a single day of lessening, and the guardians answer that their messengers came with clear proofs and that the prayer of the disbelievers is only in error. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the word "tabaan" can be a plural or a verbal noun; the grammarians of Basra take it as both singular and plural, those of Kufa as a plural without a singular, and al-Tabari concludes it is the plural of tabi'. Al-Razi suggests the followers know their leaders are powerless and aim mainly to shame them. Ibn 'Ashur sees the followers' question either as a sincere request or as a reproach.

This passage of Surah Ghafir presents a dialogue among the people of the Fire. The weak followers tell their proud leaders that they were their followers in the world and ask whether they can bear any part of the punishment for them. The leaders reply that they are all in the Fire and that God has judged among the servants, so that each receives what he deserves and no one can escape that judgment. The commentators agree on this general meaning and on the futility of the debate for the wrongdoers. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the word "tabaan" (followers) can be singular or plural: the grammarians of Basra take it as both, those of Kufa as a plural without a singular, and al-Tabari holds it to be the plural of "tabi'". For "kullun", the common reading is the nominative as subject, while Ibn al-Sumayfa' reads the accusative as emphasis on the pronoun of "inna". Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya report that the answer means God renders to each his due and does not hold anyone accountable for another's sin. The same sources connect the scene to the request of the damned to the guardians of Hell, who answer with a rebuke for not having received the prophets' clear signs, and they state that the supplication of the disbelievers is in vain. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi also note that this passage has been cited as evidence for the punishment of the grave.

This verse reports what the people of the Fire say to the guardians of Hell, the angels appointed to punish them: they ask them to call upon their Lord to lighten the torment for them by a single day. The commentators explain that this day means a span equal to one day of the worldly life, since the Hereafter has no night. They agree that the request comes after the damned have despaired, and that they turn to the angels because they consider them closer to God. The answer takes the form of rebuke and reminder: messengers came to you with clear proofs, they admit it, and the guardians reply, then call upon Him yourselves, for the supplication of the disbelievers is nothing but error. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya understand that this plea is not answered and that the unbelievers gain nothing from it. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that the command to call is not meant to secure any benefit but to show their hopelessness, since if the honoured angel is not heard, how could the disbeliever be heard. Al-Razi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi also note that this reply might come directly from God. Ibn 'Ashur sees the question as a confirmatory interrogation meant to humiliate them, and notes that the verbal form expresses the certainty of the messengers' coming. Ibn 'Uthaymin observes that a disbeliever's supplication is answered only in cases of distress or of being wronged, though this point rests on other evidence rather than on the verse itself.

This verse records the exchange between the inhabitants of Hell and its guardians. They ask the guardians to plead with their Lord to lighten their punishment by a single day. The guardians answer with a rebuke: did not your messengers come to you with clear proofs? They admit that they did, and the guardians tell them to pray themselves, concluding that the prayer of the disbelievers is only in error and goes nowhere. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi understand the guardians' words as a way of humiliating them and crushing their hope, with no real intention of helping them. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi take the phrase "pray then" as mockery. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the guardians are the angels closest to God, so the damned turned to them first. Al-Razi says the guardians refuse to intercede because intercession is only for a believer and only with God's permission. On the closing sentence, most commentators attach it to the guardians' speech, while others take it as God's own words. Al-Shawkani and Ibn 'Ashur extend it to all prayer by disbelievers, in this world and the next. Ibn Kathir holds that the prayers of disbelievers are not answered, while Ibn 'Ashur adds that rare apparent answers are coincidences with another person's prayer. Al-Qurtubi and al-Razi also cite the hadith on the prayer of the wronged person, and al-Sha'rawi and Ibn 'Uthaymin note the exceptions of the one in distress and the wronged person.

This verse states that God helps His messengers and those who believe in them in this worldly life and on the Day when the witnesses stand. The commentators differ on the nature of this help. Abu al-Aliya, al-Tabari and al-Mawardi understand it as the victory of proof and the establishment of the truth, while al-Suddi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as avenging the enemies: when a people kills a prophet or a caller to truth, God raises someone to avenge them, so the believers are victorious even when slain. Ibn Abbas speaks of dominance and subjugation, al-Dahhak of proof in this life and excuse in the next. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi note that this help can take the form of raising a cause to power, as with David, Solomon and Muhammad, of deliverance with the destruction of opponents, as with Noah and Moses, or of vengeance after the prophets' death, as with the killers of Yahya. As for the witnesses, Mujahid and al-Suddi identify them as angels who testify that the prophets delivered the message and that the peoples rejected it. Qatada adds the prophets, and Zayd ibn Aslam includes believers and the body parts. Linguistically, al-Tabari regards the readings with ya and ta for both yaqum and yanfa'u as two well-known readings with the same meaning. The verse concludes that on that Day the excuses of wrongdoers will not benefit them, that they will be cursed and will have the evil abode, which is the Fire.

This verse states that on the Day of Judgment the wrongdoers will gain nothing from their excuses, because those excuses will be false and will not be accepted. They will be cursed, meaning distanced from God's mercy, and their abode will be evil, which the commentators identify as Hell. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, understand the excuses that will fail to be the lies of the polytheists, such as swearing that they were never idolaters, since God has already established the proof against them in this world. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya propose a further possibility, that they will not be permitted to offer any excuse at all, a reading supported by a verse in al-Mursalat, and Ibn Juzayy considers this the more likely. On recitation, the readers differ between the yā' and the tā' in the verb 'does not benefit'; al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi regard both as correct and equivalent in meaning, since the feminine gender of the excuse is not real and a word intervenes. Regarding the particle 'lahum', al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan read it as meaning what is rightfully theirs, while others take it to mean 'upon them'. Commentators also differ on the phrase 'evil abode': Ibn 'Atiyya reads it as the evil outcome of the abode, while Ibn 'Uthaymin takes it to refer to the punishment within. All agree that the wrongdoers here are the disbelievers and that the verse belongs to the wider passage on God's support of His messengers and believers in this world and the next.

This verse states that God gave Moses guidance, meaning the miracles, the Torah and the laws by which people are guided, and that He left the Book to the Children of Israel, who inherited it from generation to generation. It is a guidance and a reminder for people of understanding. Most commentators understand the Book to be the Torah, while Ibn al-Sa'ib, quoted by Ibn al-Jawzi, includes the Gospel and the Psalms as well. Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir describe it as a reminder for the wise who act upon what it contains. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari also note that the word 'inherited' may mean that God gave them the land of Pharaoh, or simply that He left them the Book after Moses, depending on whether the verb is read as possession or transmission. The verse belongs to a passage on God's support for His messengers and believers. Al-Razi lists several forms of this victory, linking them to this life and the Hereafter. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the example of Moses an image of the victory granted to Muhammad and his companions. The commentators also discussed the grammatical role of the words 'guidance' and 'reminder', which may be read as a purpose complement or as a circumstantial state. Jurists draw no particular ruling from this verse.

This verse states that God gave Moses guidance, meaning the clear signs, the miracles and the Torah, and that He made the Book an inheritance for the Children of Israel. It was a guidance that explained the matters of their religion and its obligations, and a reminder for people of sound minds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi identify the Book as the Torah, passed down from generation to generation, while Ibn al-Jawzi notes that some also include the Gospel and the Psalms. Al-Tabari takes guidance to mean the clarification of the religion, whereas Ibn Qutayba and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as deliverance from error. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi see the two words as expressing direction and reminder, and the people of understanding as those who believe in and act upon the Book. Al-Razi distinguishes guidance, which is a proof, from reminder, which recalls what was forgotten. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the Torah contains both knowledge not otherwise known and a reminder of what scholars already knew. In the context of the surah, the verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ: God has aided His messengers before him, and what follows calls him to patience and to seeking forgiveness and glorifying God.

In this verse God commands His Prophet ﷺ to be patient with his people's hostility, affirming that God's promise is true and will not fail. The commentators do not all understand this promise in the same way. Muqatil takes it as the punishment of the Meccan disbelievers promised in two verses, Yahya ibn Sallam as the reward of believers in the hereafter, and al-Kalbi holds that the verse on fighting abrogated the command to endure patiently. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Ashur read it as the support and elevation of the Prophet and of God's word. As for seeking forgiveness, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir see it as an act of worship that raises rank and serves as a model for others, while others link it to the sin of the community or to leaving aside what is better, and Ibn Ashur sees it as thanks for the victory. On glorifying God in the evening and the morning, al-Hasan and Qatada take it as the afternoon and dawn prayers, Ibn Abbas as the five daily prayers, and Mujahid as the period from the sun's decline to sunset and the beginning of the day. Al-Hasan also mentions two units of prayer morning and evening before the five prayers were made obligatory. All agree that the passage consoles the Prophet. The following verse, about those who dispute God's signs without authority, is explained by most as the pride of the Quraysh, while Abu al-Aliya and Ka'b al-Ahbar apply it to the Jews who awaited the Dajjal.

This verse describes those who dispute the signs of God, meaning His proofs and Scriptures, without any authority that has come to them from Him. The commentators explain that only arrogance in their hearts drives them to it. Most agree that this arrogance is the desire for leadership and superiority over the Prophet ﷺ and his followers, so that they refuse to submit to him. Al-Tabari takes it as envy of the favour God gave the Prophet, and holds that what they covet is beyond their reach. Mujahid understands it as the greatness the Quraysh felt, al-Hasan as their hope that the Prophet and his companions would perish, and Ibn Qutayba as their attempt to overcome him. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir stress the wish to lead, to command, or to receive prophethood for themselves out of envy. Some reports, cited by Muqatil, Abu al-Aliya and Ka'b, attribute the verse to Jews who exalted the false messiah, the Dajjal, and expected him to restore their rule. Ibn Kathir calls this view strange and forced, while al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi record it without rejecting it. Several exegetes note that the dispute covers both the signs of creation and the revealed rulings, and that the phrase "without authority" describes what they actually do rather than setting an exception. The verse ends by commanding the Prophet to seek refuge in God, who hears what they say and sees what they do.

This verse states that the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of humankind, and the commentators have read it in several ways. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy, Ibn 'Ashur and most exegetes take it as an argument for the resurrection: whoever created this vast universe is all the more able to recreate people after death, since recreation is easier than original creation. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Sa'di stress that the argument concerns the greatness of the creation rather than the size of bodies. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain that the disbelievers already admitted that God created the heavens and the earth, so they were held to their own concession. Abu al-'Aliya, followed by Mawardi, Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, takes "mankind" to mean the Dajjal, while Yahya ibn Salam understands it as the re-creation of people; Mawardi adds a third reading concerning human power and the humbling of unbelievers.

The commentators agree on the meaning of the closing phrase: most people do not know, that is, they do not reflect or reason, because heedlessness dominates them and they follow their desires. Ibn 'Ashur identifies them as the polytheists of Mecca, while Ibn 'Atiyya sees "most people" as contrasted with the small number who know. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya also record the readings of the verb "remember": the ya' form is that of most readers of Medina and Basra, the ta' form that of the readers of Kufa, and Tabari considers both acceptable.

The commentators explain that the verse uses the image of the blind man, who sees nothing, and the seeing man, who sees what is before him. Just as these two are not equal, the believer who reflects on God's signs, takes them to heart and does good deeds is not the same as the disbeliever or the evildoer who turns away from them. Al-Tabari explains that the blind man stands for the unbeliever who does not reflect on the proofs, and the seeing man for the believer who perceives in them God's oneness and power. The verse closes by remarking how few people take heed. Al-Tabari and al-Nasafi note that both readings, the second person (tatadhakkarun), used by the Kufans, and the third person (yatadhakkarun), used by the others, are valid, while Ibn Atiyya observes that the third person is more common.

The commentators agree that the verse belongs to the argument for the resurrection: the One who created the heavens and the earth can recreate human beings, even though most people do not realise it. Ibn Kathir notes that many Arabs acknowledged that God created the heavens and the earth while denying the resurrection. Al-Razi argues that envy and pride blind the heart, so that the ignorant believe they possess knowledge and the sinner believes he is doing good.

Opinions differ on who the disputants are. Muqatil and Abu al-Aliya identify them as Jews who exalted the Dajjal, Yahya ibn Salam sees them as deniers of the resurrection among the Quraysh, and Ibn al-Jawzi reports these views while preferring the first. Ibn Ashur takes the address to include both polytheists and believers. Ibn Uthaymin stresses that good deeds rest on sincerity toward God and conformity to the Prophet's example.

This verse affirms that the Hour, meaning the Resurrection and Judgement, is certainly coming with no doubt about it, yet most people do not believe. Al-Tabari explains that it is the Hour in which God will raise the dead for reward and punishment, so people should be certain of its coming and repent; he identifies the majority addressed as the Quraysh who deny resurrection. Ibn Kathir, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn Sa'di explain that people fail to believe through heedlessness or arrogance, and that their minds are fixed on what they perceive with their senses. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi say that there is no doubt because a recompense must necessarily take place. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi link the verse to the argument that the One who created the heavens and the earth, far greater than mankind, is able to recreate humans; al-Razi adds that this clear proof is hidden from most people because of envy and pride. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the statement that there is no doubt concerns the coming of the Hour, which the evidence makes clear. The commentators broadly agree on the core meaning, and their differences concern how to read the negation of doubt and the function of the preceding argument. Variant readings of the verb in the following verse do not change the main sense.

The commentators explain that this verse calls people to invoke God and worship Him, promises a response to whoever calls upon Him, and threatens that those who are too proud to worship Him will enter Hell in humiliation. Most agree that the word "invoke" here includes worship: "worship Me and I will reward you", or "affirm My oneness and I will forgive you", a reading transmitted from Ibn Abbas and Mujahid and repeated by al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi. They rely on the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, "Supplication is worship", which Ibn Kathir takes as the very explanation of the verse. Al-Sudi and those who follow him read it as asking: "ask Me and I will give you". Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi consider that pride in refusing to supplicate fits the context of verses about those who dispute God's signs better. Ibn Juzayy judges the first reading the clearest, since supplication displays the servant's need before his Lord. Many scholars, including al-Qurtubi and al-Shinqiti, hold that the answer is subject to God's will. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes worshipful invocation from invocation of request and lists conditions for an answer, such as lawful food and an attentive heart. Al-Jaza'iri adds that one should not ask for sin or exceed the limits in prayer. Ibn 'Ashur connects the verse to what precedes it, as a warning against neglecting to call upon God. The following verse recalls the blessings of night and day. The commentators do not differ on the meaning of the humiliation mentioned at the end.

This verse reminds people that God made the night a time of rest in which the body recovers from the day's exertion, and made the day bright so that people can see and go about their livelihood, and that He is abundantly gracious to humanity, though most people do not give thanks. The commentators agree on the general meaning: night is for rest, day is for work and sight, and the verse is a reminder of God's favours that calls for worship of Him alone. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi stress this reminder of blessings and God's oneness in worship. Al-Mawardi offers three understandings of the night's rest: resting from the day's labour, refraining from seeking provision, or taking stock of one's deeds during the day; he also gives two readings of the day's sight: seeing God's power in creation, or seeing the means of earning a living. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that attributing sight to the day is figurative, meaning that people see in it. Al-Zamakhshari also explains the repetition of the word 'people' as a way of singling out those who are ungrateful for God's favour. Al-Razi discusses how sleep restores strength and sees in the alternation of night and day evidence for the existence of the Creator. Ibn 'Ashur reads the verse both as a reminder of blessings and as an argument for God's sole authority over creation and its management. The commentators do not differ on the core meaning, only on the rhetorical nuances and the readings the words allow.

This verse affirms that God is your Lord and the Creator of all things, that there is no deity but Him, and then asks how the listeners can turn away from Him. The commentators explain that the word 'yu'fakun' means being turned away from the truth despite clear proofs, just as earlier peoples who denied God's signs were turned away. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that those who worship other than God go astray through ignorance and desire, without any proof. Al-Mawardi gives three meanings of the word: being turned away, being denied in the matter of monotheism, or deviating from the truth. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi see the attributes 'God, your Lord, Creator of all things, there is no god but Him' as successive predicates that together gather divinity, lordship, creation and oneness. Some readers recite 'khaliqa' in the accusative, which makes 'there is no god but He' a conclusion, as Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi note. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that 'all things' refers to created beings rather than to God's attributes, and he allows that the verse may recall the resurrection. Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and Ibn 'Abbas report that the profession 'there is no god but God' is to be followed by 'Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds'. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the demonstrative 'that' points to the obvious divinity of God, which rebukes the confusion of the listeners.

The commentators explain that verse 63 of Surat Ghafir compares the turning away of the Quraysh from the truth to the turning away of the earlier nations, and that its cause is denying Allah's signs and proofs. Al-Tabari reads it as meaning: just as you have turned from the truth to falsehood, so those before you turned away, and you have taken the same misguided path. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand the verb yu'fak as being diverted from the truth even when the proofs are established, and say that anyone who denies Allah's signs without reflection or a search for truth is diverted in the same way. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the preceding question, how are you turned away, is a rebuke, and that the particle kadhalika draws a comparison with the aversion just mentioned. Al-Razi holds that the signs themselves, in the alternation of night and day, establish God's oneness, and that denial blinds the believer to the truth. Al-Shawkani and Ibn Sa'di see this turning away as a divine punishment for stubborn denial. Ibn 'Uthaymin specifies that the signs are both cosmic and revealed, and that denial means disbelief. Most commentators draw no legal ruling from this verse and explain it through the neighbouring verses on supplication and monotheism.

This verse recalls God's blessings upon people: He made the earth a stable resting place and the sky a raised structure above you. He gave you a fine form, and the commentators agree that the human form is the most beautiful among living creatures. Ibn 'Abbas notes that a human eats with the hand while standing upright, whereas other creatures eat with the mouth. God also provided good and pleasant things as provision. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir conclude that these blessings show that God alone is the Lord who deserves worship. Al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi offer related explanations of the wording, and al-Razi groups these signs into those of the horizons and those of the self. On the meaning of 'good things', Ibn Juzayy, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan explain that in a context of blessing it means what is pleasant, while in a context of permitted and forbidden it means what is lawful. On 'qarar', al-Razi and Ibn Kathir link it to the earth being firm, not shaking its inhabitants, a point Ibn 'Uthaymin supports by citing the mountains that prevent the earth from swaying, though he declines to settle the question of whether the earth moves. On 'tabarak', Ibn Kathir understands exaltation and holiness, while al-Razi gives permanence or abundance of good. Finally, many narrators, including Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, report that after saying 'there is no god but God' one should add 'Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds', which al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari take as the sense of the verse, while others treat the praise as a separate sentence.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that God is the Living who never dies, that there is no deity worthy of worship besides Him, and that believers should call upon Him and worship Him with sincere devotion, praising Him by saying, Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi, hold that this life is the complete and eternal life belonging to God by His essence, while all other life is accidental and perishable. They also agree that the calling upon God includes both worship and petition, and that sincerity means purifying the act from all association, whether open or hidden, and from showing off, as Ibn 'Ashur explains. Regarding the phrase of praise, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Sirin report that whoever says there is no god but God should follow it with Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, while others regard the praise as a separate statement. Al-Qurtubi and al-Shawkani cite hadiths on the merit of supplication. Grammarians differ on the predicate of la ilaha, which Ibn 'Uthaymin takes to be haqq (true), though the exegetes do not settle the matter. Al-Sudi understands calling upon God as asking, and al-Thawri as abandoning sins.

In this verse the Prophet is told to declare that he has been forbidden to worship those whom the idolaters invoke besides God, now that clear proofs have come to him from his Lord, and that he has been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds. Al-Tabari, al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti, and Ibn Kathir, understand these clear proofs as the signs and evidence of God's oneness, while al-Nasafi mentions the Quran, or alternatively reason and revelation.
