Al-Tabari, al-Sam'ani and Ibn Sa'di understand submission as humbling oneself and obeying God, and Ibn Sa'di adds that it involves the heart, the tongue and the limbs. Most commentators link the verse to the preceding verses, which describe God creating man from dust, then from a drop and a clot, through infancy, maturity and old age, and His power to give life and death. From this they conclude that worship belongs to Him alone (Ibn Kathir, al-Razi, al-Nasafi, al-Baghawi). Al-Baghawi notes that the words were revealed when the Prophet was invited back to disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari asks why the prohibition is attributed to revelation when reason already shows it, and answers that revelation reinforces the rational proofs, whereas Abu Hayyan holds that the prohibition rests on revelation even though reason confirms it. Ibn Ashur explains that the verse addresses the idolaters indirectly, through the Prophet's own prohibition. Ibn Uthaymin distinguishes the legal sense of Islam, an act of the believer, from its cosmic sense, and notes that clearing the heart of falsehood comes before filling it with truth.

This verse reminds people that God created them from earth, meaning that He created their father Adam from it, then made their offspring form from a drop of semen, then from a clinging clot, and then brings them out as infants. He then lets them reach their full strength and reason, then become elders, while some die before that. All this is so they reach a fixed term they cannot pass, and so that they reason and reflect on God's signs. Commentators such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy agree that the verse calls people to recognise the Creator's power and to worship Him alone. Ibn Kathir adds that death can come at any stage, even before birth. On the meaning of the "age of full strength" (ashudd), opinions differ: Ibn al-Jawzi reports several estimates, thirty, forty, twenty or eighteen years, and considers the last ones weak, while most scholars take it to be between thirty and forty. Readings of the word "elders" (shuyukh) are noted by al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan. Al-Razi argues that "earth" refers not only to Adam but to the whole chain of nourishment rooted in the soil, a view others reject in favour of Adam alone. Al-Razi, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qasimi note that the order of life's stages accords with reason. The passage continues into the next verses, which affirm that God gives life and causes death, and that when He decrees something He says "Be" and it is.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms God's absolute power: He alone gives life and causes death, and when He decrees a matter, He says to it 'Be' and it is, without effort or difficulty, as Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di state. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that the 'fa' in 'fa-idha qada' shows that what follows results from what precedes, and that the speed of creation is conveyed through the shortest act, the word 'kun', according to al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur. The latter observes that resurrection after death is understood by analogy rather than from the literal wording, while al-Razi draws from the successive stages of human life, from dust to old age, a proof of a capable Creator, and offers several readings of 'kun', including that life enters the body in a single instant. Al-Qurtubi records Ibn 'Amir's reading that puts 'fayakunu' in the subjunctive as an answer to the imperative, and al-Shinqiti stresses that the divine word is an audible command. On the first part of the passage the commentators agree: God created man from dust, then from a drop, then from a clinging clot, then brought him forth as a child, some die before old age, so that each reaches a fixed term and reflects. For the following verses, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir identify the disputers as polytheists, whereas Ibn Sirin, cited by al-Tabari, identifies them as the Qadariyya; al-Tabari adopts Ibn Zayd's view, and Ibn 'Atiyya reports that this is the view of most exegetes.

This verse asks the Prophet to consider the strange state of those who dispute about the signs of God, that is, who reject them through contention, and how they turn away from the truth once it has been made plain. The commentators agree that it rebukes those who deny the Qur'an and what the messengers brought, and that what follows is a warning: they will learn the consequence of their denial when shackles are around their necks and chains drag them through boiling water and then they are cast into the Fire. They will be asked where the gods they associated with God are, and will answer that these have forsaken them. They will be told that this punishment is the price of their vain joy and insolence, and they will enter the gates of Hell to abide there.

The scholars differ over who is meant. Ibn Zayd and most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, identify them as the polytheists who denied the Qur'an and the earlier revelations. Ibn Sirin and others reported that the verse concerns the Qadariyya, or more broadly the people of desires, with Ibn Sirin saying he did not know who else it could be about; al-Tabari cites a narration on this from Uqba ibn Amir. Al-Tabari prefers the view of Ibn Zayd, based on the words that follow about rejecting the Book, while Ibn 'Atiyya considers the other view far-fetched given the apparent sense.

The grammatical and recitation points also receive attention. The majority reading puts the word for chains in the nominative, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud read it in the accusative, and al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain the genitive reading as agreement by meaning. Mujahid explained the verb for being kindled as meaning that they become fuel for the fire, and al-Suddi as meaning that they are burned.

The commentators explain that this verse is a threat addressed to the polytheists and to those who denied the Qur'an and what the messengers brought, especially monotheism and resurrection. Its meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection they will come to know the reality of their denial, when shackles are around their necks and chains on their legs, and they are dragged through scalding water and then cast into the Fire. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand this as bodily punishment combined with moral humiliation: they will be asked where the idols they associated with God are, and they will reply that these have strayed far from them, then deny that they ever called upon anything at all. Thus God misguides the disbelievers. On the reading, the majority read 'wa-l-salasilu' in the nominative, in coordination with 'al-aghlal'. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud read it in the accusative, and al-Tabari holds the majority reading to be the correct one. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain the genitive reading as implying 'in the chains'. Opinions differ on who is meant: Ibn Zayd and the majority say the Meccan polytheists; Ibn Sirin and others say the Qadariyya; al-Tabari and others take the verse as addressing disbelievers in general. Most exegetes take 'sahb' as dragging, 'hamim' as water of extreme heat, and 'sajr' as kindling or filling. The commentators also note that 'idh' here refers to the future, the past tense being used for what is certain.

This verse describes the fate of those who denied the Book and what God sent through His messengers: they will come to know the truth of their denial when shackles are around their necks and chains on them, dragged through scalding water and then cast into the Fire. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi, understand it to refer to the polytheists who rejected the Quran, while al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir also report that Ibn Sirin and others linked it to the Qadariyya, and Ibn Zayd took it to mean the idolaters. Most agree that the word "idh" is used here for the future, the past tense signalling the certainty of what will happen, as al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Nasafi explain. On the reading of "wal-salasilu", the majority reads it in the nominative, coordinated with "al-aghlal", whereas Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud read it in the accusative with the verb "yasḥabūna" active, and al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj mention a genitive reading that Ibn al-Anbari considered unacceptable. Mujahid explains "yusjarun" as meaning they will become fuel for the Fire, while others take it to mean they will be burned. Ibn Ashur and Ibn Kathir read the verse as a threat joining pain and humiliation.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the punishment of those who denied the Book and what God sent through His messengers: iron collars are placed on their necks and chains on their legs, they are dragged through scalding water, the hamim, and then cast into the Fire, where they become its fuel. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir explain that 'yusjarun' means the fire is kindled with them, al-Sudi says they are burned, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that the Fire surrounds them and fills their insides. They agree that the verse is a threat of the Day of Resurrection, and that 'idh' carries the sense of 'idha' or a vivid present for a certain future event, as al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note.

The readings differ on 'al-salasil'. Most read it in the nominative, coordinated with 'al-aghlal'. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud read it in the accusative with an open ya, meaning they drag the chains, and Ibn 'Abbas said this is harder on them. Some read it in the genitive; al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari justify it by meaning, 'in the collars and the chains', while Ibn al-Anbari considers this construction impossible in Arabic. Ibn 'Atiyya argues the genitive coordinates with the intended sense rather than with word order.

The next verse portrays the rebuke of the polytheists, who are asked where the idols they worshipped are. They answer that the idols have strayed far from them. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that they then deny or do not recognize having worshipped anything, while Ibn al-Jawzi reports that some understand it as a deliberate denial.

As to who is meant, Ibn Zayd says the polytheists, while most exegetes, including Ibn Sirin, report that the verse concerns the Qadariyya. Ibn Kathir also adopts this view, citing Ibn Sirin and a hadith transmitted through Uqba ibn Amir.

This verse depicts the scene of the Day of Judgment in which the disbelievers are rebuked with a direct question: where are the idols and partners you used to worship besides Allah? The commentators agree that the question is one of reproach and rebuke, and that the idols refer to the deities and images they worshipped. The answer given is that their gods have gone astray from them and vanished from sight. They then move on to deny that they had ever invoked anything before. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain this denial as the panic, confusion and lying to which polytheists resort when faced with terror, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that they meant those deities were nothing that could benefit or harm. Ibn 'Ashur sees it rather as an implicit admission that these deities did not exist. As for the phrase "thus Allah misguides the disbelievers", al-Tabari reads it as a misguidance like that of their gods who abandoned them, while al-Zamakhshari understands it as a loss of access to their idols. The commentators connect this scene to the condemnation of vain joy and arrogance, and to the warning against denying the Qur'an and the messengers, the punishment being the recompense for the joy they took in falsehood in the world.

This passage describes the fate of those who denied the Book and what God sent through His messengers. The commentators differ on who they are: Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and most exegetes take them to be the polytheists who disputed God's signs, while Ibn Sirin and several exegetes, including al-Qurtubi, report that the verse was revealed concerning the Qadariyya, and Ibn Zayd identifies them as polytheists. The plain sense is that they will come to know the consequences of their denial when shackles and chains are on their necks, when they are dragged through scalding water and then cast into the fire that is kindled with them, as reported from Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. They are then rebuked by being asked where the idols they associated with God are. They answer that these have vanished from them, and then deny that they ever called upon anything. On the meaning of this denial the scholars differ: al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi, followed by most, say the idols were nothing because they neither harm nor benefit, al-Samani and al-Dimashqi read it as denial born of disbelief, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see it as an admission that their worship was void. As for the words 'thus God leads the disbelievers astray', al-Zamakhshari explains that God leads them away from their gods so that they cannot find one another, and Ibn Kathir sees it as a confirmation of their misguidance.

The commentators agree that the passage is a severe warning and rebuke, and that the punishment is both physical and mental. The following verse is read by al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya as condemning the blameworthy joy taken in falsehood, meaning shirk and sin, with 'marah' being an excessive joy; al-Dahhak, by contrast, distinguishes joy (surur) from transgression (udwan). The passage ends with the command to enter the gates of Hell to remain there, which Ibn Kathir attributes to the angels addressing them with rebuke, and which Ibn 'Ashur understands as an abode of lasting duration.

The commentators explain that God tells the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment that this punishment is the consequence of their joy in the world in what was false, in sins and in association with God, and of their exultation. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi explain the word marah as insolence, boastfulness and arrogance, while al-Dahhak takes joy to mean delight and marah to mean transgression. Most of them agree that the blameworthy joy is joy in wrongdoing, since joy in God's grace and mercy is praised, as in the verse calling people to rejoice in God's bounty and mercy. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir offer similar readings, and al-Mawardi relates the joy to the respite God had granted, which made them exult. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur present the phrase as the reason for the punishment, and Ibn 'Ashur notes that marah is an outward bearing while joy is an inner feeling. Ibn 'Uthaymin observes that the disbelievers are ordered to enter the gates of hell to remain there, making it a dreadful abode for the proud. Many commentators connect the verse to the preceding warning about those who dispute God's signs, and to the following consolation of the Prophet, who is told to be patient because God's promise is true.

This verse addresses the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, after the shackles and chains are placed on them and they are dragged through boiling water and then cast into the Fire. They are told to enter the gates of Hell, seven gates each assigned a portion of them, to remain there forever, and the verse concludes that the abode of the arrogant is a terrible one. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas explain the joy and the swagger as pride, conceit and insolence, and al-Tabari relates this to the time of polytheism. Al-Mawardi gives two readings: the joy may be contentment with the respite granted, with the swagger being insolence, or joy and aggressive transgression, as al-Dahhak holds. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the angels speak these words as reproach and mockery. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that the past tense used with the word for "when" refers to the future because the event is certain, and that the word "abode" is chosen over "entrance" because it better conveys lasting dwelling. Commentators differ on whether the command "enter" conveys humiliation or honour: Ibn 'Ashur sees a rising stage of rebuke, and Ibn 'Uthaymin reads it as humiliation. All agree that the stay is eternal, which Ibn 'Uthaymin supports with other verses.

In this verse God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to be patient in the face of the polytheists' disputing and denial, and assures him that His promise of victory over them and of punishment reaching them is certainly true. The commentators explain that "some of what We promise them" refers to punishment that befalls them during the Prophet's lifetime, such as the killing and capture at Badr, and that "or We take you back" means he dies before it reaches them, so that they return to God on the Day of Resurrection to face a more severe punishment. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir mainly take the sense of victory in this world, and Ibn Kathir adds that God delighted the Prophet's eyes by destroying the leaders of Quraysh at Badr and then conquered Mecca during his lifetime. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi hold that the answer to the first conditional is omitted and that "to Us they will be returned" answers the second, a grammatical analysis that Abu Hayyan reports and discusses. Al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di read the verse as encouragement to patience grounded in trust in the promise. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the emphasis with "inna" answers the believers' impatience at the delay of victory. Ibn 'Uthaymin connects the verse to three kinds of patience: in obedience, in restraint from sin, and in accepting divine decrees.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ that He sent many messengers before him to their peoples, some whose stories He related to him and others whose stories He did not. The commentators differ on their number: al-Tabari, al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir cite reports attributed to Anas, Salman and Ali that give different figures, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan mention an unnamed black Abyssinian prophet. Ibn Kathir notes that those whose stories are not told are far more numerous. The central meaning of the verse's second part is that no messenger could bring a sign on his own; it required God's permission. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi read this as a response to the Quraysh who demanded miracles out of obstinacy. As for the coming of God's command, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari take it to mean the Resurrection, while al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan take it to refer to the punishment at Badr. In either case, the matter is decided with truth, the messengers and believers are saved, and the deniers of truth are lost. Al-Alusi notes a report giving the number of prophets as one hundred and twenty-four thousand, but he points out that this report is not unanimously accepted, and Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that no precise figure can be relied upon.

This verse reminds the reader that God created the livestock and made it serve people: some animals are for riding, others for food, and they provide further benefits such as milk, wool, hair and hides. The commentators agree that these blessings point to God's oneness and power, and that being carried on land by these animals and at sea by ships are among the signs of God that cannot reasonably be denied.

They differ on what "al-an'am" refers to here. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Zajjaj and al-Alusi take it to mean camels alone, which fits the context of riding and carrying loads. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya broaden the term to include horses, mules and donkeys, while Ibn Kathir, Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Ashur understand it as camels, cattle and sheep together.

The preposition "min" in "minha" is also discussed. Most exegetes, such as al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and al-Jaza'iri, read it as partitive: some of the animals are for riding and others for eating. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi also allow the sense of starting point. Al-Zamakhshari explains that riding serves religious purposes such as pilgrimage, holy war and emigration in search of knowledge, whereas eating falls under permissible matters, a view al-Razi repeats. Finally, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that "'ala al-fulk" means "upon" the ships, to match the wording of the previous phrase.

This verse reminds people that God subjected livestock to them, some for riding and others for food, and that they provide further benefits such as milk, wool, hair and hides. Through them people reach distant destinations and carry their loads, and they are carried on land by them and at sea by ships. The commentators agree that these blessings are signs of God's power and oneness, and the verse ends with a rebuke to those who deny God's signs. They differ on what "al-an'am" means. Al-Zajjaj, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to mean camels mainly, since riding is most associated with them, while al-Tabari extends it to cattle, horses and mules. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi favour the eight kinds of livestock named in the Quran: camels, cattle, sheep and goats. On the phrase "a need in your breasts", Qatada and Mujahid explain it as carrying loads from one town to another, while Ibn 'Ashur reads it as intention and resolve, and Ibn 'Uthaymin adds pleasure in possession or trade. Abu al-Su'ud suggests that being carried on them may mean transporting women and children in a litter. On the choice of 'ala with the ship, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi consider both prepositions correct, while al-Alusi sees the word chosen to match the earlier 'alayha'.

The commentators explain that this verse concludes the enumeration of God's favours to humans regarding livestock. According to al-Zajjaj and others, al-an'am refers to camels, while others take it to mean the eight pairs of animals. These animals are ridden, eaten, and provide wool, hair and milk, and they carry loads on land just as ships carry them at sea. The verse then states that God shows them His signs, meaning His proofs of His oneness and perfect power, and rebukes them with a question: which of God's signs will you deny?

Al-Tabari takes these signs to be those in the heavens and the earth, while Ibn Kathir places them in the horizons and in the human self. Al-Jaza'iri holds that the signs are so evident that they cannot be denied. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi explain that the word ayya is governed by the verb tunkirun because the interrogative keeps its place at the head of the sentence, and that attaching the divine name strengthens the solemnity and the force of the rebuke. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the masculine form ayya is the common usage while the feminine is rare, a view Ibn 'Ashur repeats, stressing the indefinite nature of the word.

The commentators agree that the verse reproaches those who reject a truth that is manifest. Ibn 'Atiyya considers the meaning general, covering every lesson and every occasion for reflection. On why the purpose particle is attached only to riding and reaching needs, al-Zamakhshari answers that these aims are religious, such as pilgrimage or holy war, while eating belongs to ordinary permitted benefits. Al-Razi repeats this explanation, while Abu Hayyan finds it less convincing. These debates are grammatical and theological in nature and do not change the general sense of the verse.

This verse calls on the unbelievers to travel through the land and reflect on the fate of earlier peoples. Those peoples were more numerous, stronger and left greater traces behind them, yet their numbers, power and wealth did not help them when punishment came. The commentators agree that the travel meant is both physical and reflective, and that the traces refer to palaces, buildings and dwellings carved into mountains. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read the phrase "what availed them" as a negation, and address the verse to the Quraysh, while others read it as a question. Al-Tabari also reports Mujahid's view that the traces are the footprints of these giant peoples, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand them as buildings and fortresses.

On the phrase "they rejoiced in what knowledge they had", opinions differ. According to Mujahid, cited by Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir, the disbelievers claimed to know more than the messengers and denied resurrection and punishment. Al-Sudi held that what they called knowledge was in fact ignorance. Al-Zamakhshari also mentions the knowledge of philosophers and of worldly affairs. Ibn Zayd and others attribute the joy to the messengers, who rejoiced at the destruction of their enemies and their own deliverance.

Most exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Razi, agree that faith professed once the punishment has been seen is not accepted, relying on the story of Pharaoh and the hadith that repentance is accepted until the death rattle begins. Ibn Kathir adds that this is a constant divine way with all nations.

This passage notes that the earlier peoples who rejected their messengers were more numerous, stronger, and left more impressive traces on the earth than the Quraysh, yet their power and gains did not help them. When their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they rejoiced in what they had of knowledge, which the commentators generally regard as ignorance, and the punishment they mocked befell them. Most exegetes take the pronoun in 'they rejoiced' to refer to the disbelieving peoples, and the 'knowledge' to be their false beliefs. Mujahid, cited by Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, says they claimed: we know better than them, we will neither be resurrected nor punished; al-Sudi says they rejoiced in their ignorance; Ibn Zayd, reported by Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya, holds that they trusted their worldly learning and denied the afterlife.

Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi understand it instead as the learning of philosophers and materialists who scorned prophetic revelation, and they relate the anecdote of Socrates. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi also note the reading in which their joy was mockery of what the messengers brought. Others, such as al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, report that the pronoun refers to the messengers, who rejoiced in their own salvation and the ruin of their enemies; al-Mawardi and Abu al-Su'ud also list this as a possibility.

As for 'what they used to mock', the commentators identify it as the threatened punishment. Ibn Kathir stresses that faith professed when the punishment is seen is not accepted, citing the hadith about the dying person and the example of Pharaoh. Ibn 'Ashur notes that calling their beliefs 'knowledge' is said with irony.

This passage tells of the peoples who denied their messengers: when they saw God's violence coming upon them, they declared their faith in God alone and disavowed the idols they had associated with Him, but this late faith did not benefit them. Al-Tabari explains that "Our might" means the punishments that struck them, and that their words "We believe in God alone" acknowledge His oneness and reject the deities they had associated with Him. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi agree, reading the "might" as the severity of the torment and the association as worship of idols. About the preceding phrase, "they rejoiced in the knowledge they had", al-Mujahid reports that they said: "We know more than they do; we will neither be raised nor punished". Al-Sudi held that they took their ignorance for knowledge, and Ibn Zayd linked it to worldly knowledge. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, however, take the joy to belong to the messengers, who rejoiced at the destruction of their opponents. The commentators agree that faith professed at the sight of punishment is not accepted, since it is compelled rather than chosen, and Ibn Kathir ties this to a hadith on repentance accepted until the death rattle begins. Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Ashur present it as a constant divine law. On the grammar of "the way of God", some read it as an absolute object and others as a warning to the people of Mecca, a view Ibn 'Uthaymin prefers. The verse ends by affirming that the disbeliever is a loser at all times, and that this loss becomes plain when the punishment arrives.

This verse states that faith no longer benefits disbelievers once they witness God's punishment, and the commentators read this as a fixed divine law applied to earlier peoples. Al-Tabari, citing Qatada, explains that repentance made in the face of punishment is not accepted, and Ibn Kathir adds that this applies even to one who repents at the moment of death-rattle. The two Jalalayn explain that faith is not accepted when the punishment descends, and that the loss of the disbelievers becomes clear to all, although they had been losers all along.

Ibn Kathir links the passage to Pharaoh's words as he drowned, which were rejected. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that the word "hunalika" is used figuratively for a moment rather than a place. Al-Zajjaj, as relayed by several authors, observes that the disbeliever is a loser at all times, but that his loss becomes evident to him when the punishment is seen.

The commentators agree that compelled faith, which arises from facing punishment, does not save, unlike faith freely chosen beforehand. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi mention the people of Yunus, who believed before punishment reached them and were spared, as an exception. Al-Alusi reports an opinion that faith at the moment of punishment is accepted by God's grace, though he does not adopt it himself. Al-Razi places the criterion at the sight of signs of the hereafter and the angels of punishment.

Grammatically, most take "sunnata Allah" as an emphatic verbal noun, while some read it as a warning addressed to the people of Makkah.
